extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers interested in philosophy and psychology of humor
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedia-level survey of major philosophical and psychological theories of laughter and humor, their historical defenders and critics, and related conceptual distinctions (e.g., comedy vs tragedy, joke structure, evolutionary/play accounts). Useful for understanding criteria that diagnose, evaluate, or produce humorous effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter expresses feelings of superiority over other people or over a former state of ourselves (classical view from Plato, Hobbes, Descartes; 20th-century label: Superiority Theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains scornful or mocking laughter (examples: Plato's and Hobbes' accounts). Criticisms and counterexamples are provided (Hutcheson: superiority not necessary or sufficient; self-directed laughter, laughter at clever skill such as Chaplin, and experimental cases like Deckers’ weight study). Use with caution: good at explaining malicious laughter but fails to cover many non-scornful cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter releases pent-up nervous or psychic energy — a pressure-relief mechanism in the nervous system (accounts by Shaftesbury, Spencer, Dewey, Freud).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants: Shaftesbury's 'animal spirits', Spencer's nervous-energy discharge, Freud's detailed typology (der Witz, the comic, humor) where laughter vents repressed affects, saved cognitive energy, or unused affective energy. Examples: poetic reversals, Mark Twain story. Criticisms: hydraulic physiological model outdated; Freud’s psychoanalytic claims questioned; contemporary scholars rarely use this as a general explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises from perceiving something incongruous—violations of mental patterns or expectations (set-up violated by punch), the now-dominant theory in philosophy and psychology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical roots (Aristotle, Cicero), articulated by Beattie, Kant, Schopenhauer, Kierkegaard. Practical formulation: jokes have a set-up that creates expectation and a punch that violates it. Variants emphasize that enjoyment may be the resolution of the incongruity (Schultz, Suls). Use when designing jokes: create and then violate (or resolve) expectations; note developmental constraints (studies claim resolution becomes required after about age seven).

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-up and Punch (joke structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke typically has a set-up that creates an expectation and a punch (line) that violates that expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as the practical correlate of the Incongruity Theory (Aristotle’s advice for speakers). Used by stand-up comedians and joke writers; examples and illustrations provided. Guidance implies craft advice: build clear expectations, then deliver an unexpected ending; beware repeat exposure which reduces surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity-Resolution (two-stage) model
rubrics_metrics.description: What is enjoyed is not mere incongruity but the resolution/fitting of an anomalous element into a conceptual schema (two-stage models by Schultz, Suls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that after a certain developmental stage listeners require a cognitive resolution to 'get' the joke. Use this to design jokes whose punch can be mentally integrated (rather than merely absurd) for greater appreciation in older children/adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kantian criterion: strained expectation transformed into nothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter arises from the sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing — the dissipation of a tense expectation (Kant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant stresses this is not about feeling superior; the pleasure is a bodily excitation from shifting ideas ('play of thought'). Useful for analyzing jokes where the punch dissolves an anticipated outcome into nullity rather than replacing it with an opposite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schopenhauer's concept–perception incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises from the sudden perception of incongruity between abstract concepts and particular perceptions (the mismatch between a concept and the real objects subsumed under it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains wit as facility in finding a concept under which apparently disparate things can be subsumed; accounts for why being laughed at can feel insulting (exposes mismatch between conception and reality). Useful for producing witticisms that exploit conceptual-category slippages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freud's three laughter situations (der Witz, the comic, humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud distinguishes: der Witz (jokes/witty remarks — release of energy used for repression), the comic (release of energy normally used for thinking), and humor (release or economy of affective energy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each situation has different psychological mechanics and typical subject-matter (der Witz: sexual/hostile material; the comic: clumsy actions; humor: suppressed pity turned to pleasure). The SEP entry gives examples and critiques (e.g., professional humorists' conscious strategies contradict Freud). Use as an analytic taxonomy rather than an unquestioned production recipe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play Theory / Evolutionary account: humor as play
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor evolved from mock-aggressive play (in apes) and laughter functions as a play signal; humor is best understood as a form of play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues understanding humor as play helps explain benefits (social bonding, learning, health) and counters traditional objections. Empirical and comparative evidence (primates, play fighting) supports aspects of this account. Use when designing humor that signals friendly, nonthreatening intent (e.g., mock aggression among peers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy genre features (what makes something comical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy differs from tragedy: comedy uses common speech, broader and more social cast (family/group), often features lower-class protagonists, and emphasizes thinking over feeling (emotional disengagement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As production criteria: employ ordinary language, ensemble dynamics, situational social conflicts, and characters who reason their way through problems. These features contribute to comedy’s social inclusiveness and pragmatic effects (social lubricant, psychological benefits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vs Tragic distinction (painless vs painful contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is a painless contradiction or mistake; the tragic is a suffering contradiction that lacks a way out (Aristotle, Kierkegaard, Hazlitt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to evaluate whether a scenario is comic (invites detached amusement because there is a non-painful resolution) or tragic (elicits sorrow). Helps writers avoid turning material intended as comic into something distressing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand-up–philosophy affinities (practical criteria for good stand-up/philosophical humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven affinities that make stand-up comedy similar to philosophy: conversational interaction; reflection on familiar puzzling experiences; questioning approach ('X—what's up with that?'); emotional disengagement; critical thinking; careful attention to language; and pleasure in surprising perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As prescriptive guidelines for producing thoughtful, effective stand-up: be interactive, start from relatable puzzles, use questions as prompts, maintain some emotional distance, be critical and precise with language, and aim for surprising insights that give pleasure similar to doing philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/social constraints on humor (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical and philosophical objections to laughter emphasize its malicious, scornful, or socially corrosive forms (Plato, early Christian writers, Puritans); laughter can express hostility or contribute to harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat malicious mockery as an ethical concern: avoid punching-down, scornful laughter, and unseasonable boisterousness. The article records institutional sanctions (monastic rules, Puritan bans) as extreme historical responses; use these critiques to evaluate moral/ethical limits when producing humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological and social benefits of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor yields psychological and physical health benefits, fosters mental flexibility, and serves as a social lubricant; comedy valorizes thinking and detachment that have epistemic and therapeutic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a positive criterion when evaluating humor’s worth: consider whether a humorous piece promotes well-being, mental agility, or social bonding. The SEP links these benefits to philosophical defenses of humor and to empirical studies.
